config.title: Write typed sortBy helper

intro.title: Write typed sortBy helper
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a typed `sortBy` helper function that sorts an array of objects by a specified property. You'll learn how to use TypeScript generics to create flexible, reusable functions that maintain type safety. The core concepts involve working with arrays, object keys, and custom comparator logic. By the end, you'll have a practical utility that can sort any array of objects while ensuring your code is type-checked and error-free.
intro.usecase: The typed sortBy helper is essential in data-rich applications where users need to organize information meaningfully. In e-commerce dashboards, administrators use it to sort products by price, rating, or inventory levels with type safety. Financial platforms rely on it to order transactions by date or amount in transaction history panels. Data visualization tools implement it to arrange datasets by various metrics in interactive charts and tables, ensuring sorting logic is robust and maintainable.

objectives: Implement a generic sortBy function that accepts typed arrays and sort keys
Apply type constraints to ensure sort keys exist on array elements
Construct a comparator function that dynamically accesses nested object properties
Configure the function to handle both ascending and descending sort orders
Integrate the typed helper into existing TypeScript code with proper imports
Manipulate array data using the typed sortBy helper with different data structures
Initialize type-safe function parameters with default values for optional arguments

steps.title: Import TypeScript and declare the sortBy function signature
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript file and declare a generic sortBy function signature with proper type parameters. Start by declaring a function named 'sortBy' with two type parameters: T for the array element type and K for the key type.
steps.hint: Use the 'function' keyword followed by the function name, then type parameters in angle brackets before the parameter list.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named 'sortBy' is declared with two generic type parameters T and K, ready for implementation in later steps.
successCriteria: The sortBy function is declared with type parameters <T, K> and an empty function body.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've declared a function named 'sortBy' with two type parameters <T, K>.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function declaration is missing or incorrect. Please declare a function named 'sortBy' with two generic type parameters <T, K>.

steps.title: Define the sortBy function parameters with proper typing
steps.instruction: Add two parameters to the sortBy function: an array of type T[] and a key extractor function that takes a T item and returns a comparable value K.
steps.hint: The key extractor function should have type (item: T) => K. Remember to add these parameters inside the parentheses after the generic type parameters.
steps.expectedOutcome: The sortBy function will have properly typed parameters that accept an array and a key extraction function.
successCriteria: The sortBy function has two parameters: array of type T[] and keyExtractor of type (item: T) => K.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have both parameters: an array of T[] and a key extractor function that takes T and returns K.
steps.feedbackWrong: The parameters are missing or incorrectly typed. The function needs an array parameter and a key extractor function parameter with proper TypeScript types.

steps.title: Implement the sortBy function body with array sorting
steps.instruction: Inside the sortBy function, implement the body to sort the array using the key extractor function and return a new sorted array.
steps.hint: Use the array's slice method to create a copy, then sort it using the key extractor to compare items.
steps.expectedOutcome: The sortBy function should now have a working implementation that returns a sorted copy of the input array.
successCriteria: The function body uses slice() to copy the array and sort() with a comparator that uses keyExtractor.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're returning a sorted copy of the array, not modifying the original.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check your implementation. You need to copy the array and sort it using the key extractor function.

steps.title: Add type constraints for comparable values
steps.instruction: Add a generic constraint to the K type parameter to ensure it only accepts string, number, or boolean types.
steps.hint: Use the `extends` keyword after the type parameter to restrict it to a union of comparable types.
steps.expectedOutcome: The K type parameter will be constrained to only accept string, number, or boolean types, ensuring the key extractor returns comparable values.
successCriteria: The K type parameter has a constraint of `extends string | number | boolean`.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the constraint includes all three comparable types: string, number, and boolean.
steps.feedbackWrong: The constraint is missing or incorrect. Remember to use the `extends` keyword to restrict K to string, number, or boolean types.

steps.title: Create a test interface for demonstration
steps.instruction: Define an interface named 'User' with properties 'id' (number), 'name' (string), and 'age' (number) that will be used to test the sortBy function.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with type annotations.
steps.expectedOutcome: A User interface is created with the specified properties, ready to be used as test data for the sortBy function.
successCriteria: The User interface is defined with id: number, name: string, and age: number properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created an interface, but check that it has all three required properties with correct types: id (number), name (string), and age (number).
steps.feedbackWrong: The User interface wasn't properly defined. Make sure to use the 'interface' keyword and include all three properties with type annotations.

steps.title: Initialize test data with the interface
steps.instruction: Create an array of test objects that conform to the User interface, with mixed values for sorting. Name the array 'users'.
steps.hint: Define an array of objects where each object matches the User interface structure. Include different values for the 'name' and 'age' properties to test sorting.
steps.expectedOutcome: An array named 'users' containing multiple User objects with varying 'name' and 'age' values is created.
successCriteria: The 'users' array is defined with the correct type annotation (User[]), contains at least 3 objects, and each object has both 'name' (string) and 'age' (number) properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your array is typed as User[], contains multiple objects, and each object has both 'name' and 'age' properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The test data array isn't quite right. Remember to create an array of User objects with varying 'name' and 'age' values, and type it as User[].

steps.title: Test sortBy with string property sorting
steps.instruction: Call the sortBy function with your test data array and a key extractor that returns a string property (like 'name'), storing the result in a variable.
steps.hint: Use the sortBy function you declared earlier. Pass your test array as the first argument and a function that returns item.name as the second argument. Assign the result to a new variable.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: calling a typed helper function
const sortedNumbers = sortBy([3, 1, 2], (num) => num);
steps.expectedOutcome: The sortBy function is called with test data and a string property extractor, demonstrating its usage with string keys.
successCriteria: sortBy is called with the test array and a key extractor function that returns a string property, and the result is stored in a variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling sortBy with both arguments: the test array and a function that returns a string property like 'name'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The sortBy function call is missing or incorrect. Remember to pass your test array and a key extractor function that returns a string property.

steps.title: Add console logging to verify sorting results
steps.instruction: Add console.log statements after each sortBy call to display both the original test data and the sorted results.
steps.hint: Use console.log with descriptive messages to output the arrays. Place them right after the sortBy calls you already have.
steps.expectedOutcome: The console will display the original test array and the sorted arrays, showing that sortBy works correctly with both string and number properties.
successCriteria: Two console.log statements are added: one for the original test data and one for each sorted result.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some logging, but make sure to log both the original test data and each sorted array result.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try adding console.log statements after each sortBy call to output the arrays for verification.

steps.title: Test with invalid key to demonstrate type safety
steps.instruction: Attempt to call the sortBy function with a property key that doesn't exist on your User interface, such as 'invalidKey', to observe TypeScript's compile-time error detection.
steps.hint: Add a line that tries to call sortBy with a key extractor that returns a property not defined in your User interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will see a TypeScript compilation error when trying to access a property that doesn't exist on the interface, demonstrating how TypeScript catches type errors at compile time.
successCriteria: The code includes an attempt to call sortBy with a key extractor that references a property not defined in the User interface, resulting in a TypeScript error.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a call to sortBy, but make sure you're trying to access a property that doesn't exist on your User interface (like 'invalidKey') to trigger the TypeScript error.
steps.feedbackWrong: The code doesn't include an attempt to call sortBy with an invalid property key. Try adding a line that uses a property not defined in your User interface to see TypeScript's error detection.
